stem: A 2-year-old boy has his second episode of invasive pneumococcal infection (pneumonia with bacteraemia). His parents report that he hardly had a fever during either episode, and the local signs of inflammation were mild. He has had several common viral infections without complications. Which defect best explains this picture?

options.text: Loss-of-function mutation in TLR3
options.explanation: TLR3 loss of function gives recurrent herpes simplex encephalitis, not invasive pyogenic infection.

options.text: Mutation in the IL-12 receptor β1 chain
options.explanation: IL-12Rβ1 mutations give susceptibility to Salmonella and mycobacteria, not pneumococcal 'cold' infection.

options.text: Autosomal recessive IRAK4 deficiency
options.explanation: MyD88/IRAK4 deficiency gives severe invasive bacterial (especially pneumococcal) infections early in life with little fever or inflammation; viral susceptibility is not increased.

options.text: Gain-of-function mutation in NLRP3
options.explanation: NLRP3 gain of function (CAPS) gives excess IL-1 with fever and rash, the opposite of a fever-poor picture.

options.text: Homozygous mutation in UNC93B
options.explanation: UNC93B deficiency impairs endosomal TLRs and type I IFN and predisposes to herpes simplex encephalitis.

stem: A 6-year-old girl is admitted with her second episode of herpes simplex virus-1 encephalitis. She has no history of severe bacterial, fungal or other viral infections. Immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets are normal. A defect in which pathway is most likely?

options.text: MyD88–IRAK4 signalling to NF-κB
options.explanation: MyD88/IRAK4 defects give invasive pyogenic bacterial infections; IRAK4 deficiency adds no viral susceptibility.

options.text: TLR5 recognition of bacterial flagellin
options.explanation: TLR5 is a surface receptor for flagellin of motile bacteria and has no role in herpes simplex encephalitis in the sources.

options.text: NOD2 recognition of muramyl dipeptide
options.explanation: NOD2 senses bacterial peptidoglycan (MDP); its variants relate to Crohn's disease and Blau syndrome.

options.text: Lectin pathway initiation by MBL
options.explanation: Low MBL increases risk of various infections mainly when other immune defects coexist; it does not cause isolated HSE.

options.text: Endosomal TLR3–TRIF signalling to type I IFN
options.explanation: Defects in TLR3, UNC93B, TRIF, TRAF3 or TBK1 impair type I IFN downstream of TLR3 and cause herpes simplex encephalitis without broad viral susceptibility.

stem: A 34-year-old man has had attacks since childhood of fever, urticarial rash, joint pain and conjunctivitis. The attacks start a few hours after cold exposure. His father has the same attacks. Which mechanism best explains his disease?

options.text: Gain-of-function NLRP3 mutation with excess inflammasome-generated IL-1β
options.explanation: Dominant NLRP3 (cryopyrin) mutations cause CAPS; in FCAS cold exposure triggers fever, urticarial rash, joint pain and conjunctivitis.

options.text: MEFV mutation with dysregulated pyrin inflammasome
options.explanation: FMF (MEFV/pyrin) presents with fever, serositis and arthritis, without cold-induced urticarial rash.

options.text: TNFRSF1A mutation affecting TNF receptor I
options.explanation: TRAPS gives periodic fever, myalgia and rash; cold triggering is not a feature in the sources.

options.text: Gain-of-function NOD2 mutation with excess NF-κB
options.explanation: NOD2 gain of function causes Blau syndrome with spontaneous inflammation of joints, eyes and skin.

options.text: Partial loss of mevalonate kinase activity
options.explanation: HIDS gives fever from infancy with high serum IgD and lymphadenopathy.

stem: A 58-year-old man has a third attack of acute monoarthritis of the first toe. Joint aspirate shows monosodium urate crystals. He does not respond to conventional anti-inflammatory drugs, and the rheumatologist proposes IL-1 blockade. Which innate mechanism explains why IL-1 blockade is effective?

options.text: Urate crystals bind TLR4 and signal through MyD88 alone
options.explanation: TLR4 recognizes LPS (with MD2) and heat shock proteins; the sources link urate crystals to the inflammasome, not to TLR4.

options.text: Cytosolic DNA from crystals activates cGAS–STING
options.explanation: cGAS–STING senses cytosolic dsDNA and induces type I IFN, not IL-1β.

options.text: NOD2 in Paneth cells recognizes urate and activates RIP2
options.explanation: NOD2 recognizes muramyl dipeptide from bacterial peptidoglycan and activates NF-κB through RIP2.

options.text: Phagocytosed crystals damage lysosomes and activate NLRP3–caspase-1
options.explanation: Urate crystals damage lysosomes and activate the NLRP3 inflammasome; caspase-1 then generates active IL-1β. IL-1 antagonists treat severe resistant gout.

options.text: Cytosolic urate activates caspase-4 and caspase-5 directly
options.explanation: The noncanonical caspase-4/5 pathway is activated by cytosolic LPS, not by urate.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with gram-negative urosepsis has a plasma CRP that rises steeply over 48 hours. Which group of cytokines, produced after TLR4 recognition of LPS, mainly drives this hepatic CRP synthesis?

options.text: IL-12 and IL-18
options.explanation: IL-12 and IL-18 mainly drive IFN-γ production and NK cell function, not acute-phase protein synthesis.

options.text: IL-6, IL-1 and TNF
options.explanation: IL-6, IL-1 and TNF induce hepatocytes to make acute-phase proteins; CRP can rise up to 1000-fold.

options.text: IFN-α and IFN-β
options.explanation: Type I IFNs induce an antiviral state and more MHC class I; they are not the drivers of CRP synthesis.

options.text: IL-33 released as an alarmin
options.explanation: IL-33 is an epithelial alarmin released from damaged cells; it is not the hepatic acute-phase signal.

options.text: CXCL8 and CCL2
options.explanation: These chemokines recruit neutrophils and monocytes; they do not induce hepatic acute-phase proteins.

stem: A 5-month-old girl has recurrent fever, skin lesions due to cutaneous vasculopathy, and tachypnoea. Chest CT shows interstitial lung disease. Infection screening is negative. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.text: Gain-of-function NLRP3 with excess IL-1β
options.explanation: CAPS gives fever, neutrophilic rash, bony lesions and CNS inflammation, not vasculopathy with interstitial lung disease.

options.text: Loss-of-function TLR3 with low type I IFN
options.explanation: TLR3 loss of function gives herpes simplex encephalitis, not a sterile inflammatory disease.

options.text: Loss-of-function MyD88 with absent NF-κB signalling
options.explanation: MyD88 deficiency gives invasive pyogenic infections with little inflammation.

options.text: Gain-of-function NOD2 with excess NF-κB signalling
options.explanation: NOD2 gain of function causes Blau syndrome with inflammation of joints, eyes and skin.

options.text: Gain-of-function STING with excess type I IFN
options.explanation: STING gain of function causes SAVI, an interferonopathy with cutaneous vasculopathy, fever and interstitial lung disease.

stem: Toll-like receptors. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.text: TLR9 sits in endosomes and recognizes unmethylated CpG DNA.
options.explanation: TLR9 is endosomal and binds unmethylated CpG motifs, common in prokaryotic DNA but rare in vertebrate DNA.

options.text: For LPS recognition, the accessory protein MD2 binds lipid A and the complex engages TLR4.
options.explanation: MD2 binds the lipid A component of LPS and the complex interacts with TLR4; CD14 is also needed for efficient signalling.

options.text: TLR5 sits in endosomes and recognizes viral single-stranded RNA.
options.explanation: TLR5 is a plasma membrane TLR that binds bacterial flagellin; TLR7 and TLR8 bind ssRNA.

options.text: TLR3 depends on MyD88 to induce IFN-β.
options.explanation: TLR3 is the only TLR that does not use MyD88; it signals only through TRIF.

stem: NOD-like receptors and inflammasomes. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.text: Caspase-1 cleaves gasdermin D, and the N-terminal fragment forms pores in the plasma membrane.
options.explanation: The gasdermin D N-terminal fragment polymerizes into pores through which IL-1β leaves the cell.

options.text: Neutrophils are the main cell type that dies by pyroptosis.
options.explanation: Pyroptosis affects macrophages and dendritic cells, not neutrophils.

options.text: NOD2 recognizes muramyl dipeptide, and some NOD2 polymorphisms increase the risk of Crohn's disease.
options.explanation: NOD2 senses MDP from gram-negative and gram-positive peptidoglycan; some variants raise Crohn's risk.

options.text: In humans, cytosolic LPS can activate caspase-4 or caspase-5 and cause pyroptosis.
options.explanation: This is the noncanonical inflammasome pathway (caspase-11 in rodents).

stem: Soluble PRRs and cytosolic nucleic-acid sensors. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.text: CRP binds phosphorylcholine and activates the classical complement pathway by binding C1q.
options.explanation: CRP binds phosphorylcholine; CRP, SAP and PTX3 activate the classical pathway through C1q.

options.text: Ficolins recognize carbohydrates through a C-type lectin domain, like MBL.
options.explanation: Ficolins have a fibrinogen-type recognition domain instead of a C-type lectin domain.

options.text: RIG-I recognizes viral RNA with a 5′-triphosphate, which capped host mRNA lacks.
options.explanation: RIG-I only recognizes RNA with a 5′-triphosphate; host mRNA carries a 7-methylguanosine cap.

options.text: MAVS is an endoplasmic reticulum adaptor that binds cGAMP.
options.explanation: STING is the ER adaptor that binds cGAMP; MAVS is on the outer mitochondrial membrane and serves RIG-I and MDA5.
